FOREWORD 



Refractories are the primary materials used in the construction of all furnaces 
in the ferrous and non-ferrous industries. These are used in the lining of laddies, 
hot metal mixers» metal retaining vessels, and flues and stacks through which hot 
gasses pass. Refractories are also used for lining of boilers, pressure vessels, kilns 
and vessels using hot fliitds at various temperatures. In short, refractories can be 
termed as the nxate.riat of construction exposed to high temperatures and corroding 
atmospheres, and they retain their shapes and characteristics without reacting 
with the molten material or the corroding atmospheres. 

Refractory materials are costly and a sudden failure of any refractory may 
result in great loss of time, product and equipment. Therefore, the selection of 
refractories suitable for a particular application is of paramount importance. 
Cost-benefit-analysis is often the basis of selection ^f such refractories. A refractory 
best suited for an application may not necessarily have the longest life. In 
selecting the proper refractory, a balance is struck between the initial installed 
cost and in-service performance. 

Steel industry uses over 70 percent of the refractories consumed in the country. 
However, integrated steel plants employ a team of refractory engineers and 
specialists for selection and use of refractories. On the other hand, non-ferrous 
sector, glass industry, and other high temiperature and corrosion intensive 
industries do not always employ refractory specialists. The application of 
refractories in such industries is nevertheless very critical and any premature 
failure may lead to long down times and loss of production. 

With the above problems of unorganized sector in mind, the Refractories 
Sectional Committee ( SMDG 18 ) decided to bring out a handbook for refrac- 
tories which could be used as a reference book by the unorganized sector. The 
Refractories Sectional Committee, allotted this work to a specially constituted 
Panel ( SMDG 18 : P6 ) consisting of experts from various fields of activities 
which the handbook will eventually cover. The work of this panel would also 
lead to improvement of refractory engineering practices and overall conservation 
of materials and energy. 

The Handbook will be published in parts; each part dealing with particular 
industry/process. It is intended to cover the refractories used in the following 
industries: 

a) Cement kiln systems ( large plants ); 

b) Mini-cement plants; 

c) Petroleum and petro-chemical industry; 

d) Pulp and paper industry; 

e) Lime kilns — rotary type and shaft type; 

f ) Primary processing of non-ferrous materials, such as, aluminium, copper, 
zinc, lead, etc; 

g) Manufacture of ferro-alloys; 

h) Pouring practices for ferrous and non-ferrous materials; 
j) Incinerators; 

k) Ceramic and refractory industry; 
m) Nuclear fuel plants; 
n) Glass industry; 
p) Glass fibre industry; and 
q) Iron and steel industry. 



Each part of the Handbook will cover the following aspects of the refractory 
.engineering: 

a) Process of manufacture used; 

b) Types of boilers/furnaces systems; 

c) Objectives of the refractory lining; 

d) Design engineering features of the furances; 

e) Principal zones and sections of the furnaces; 

f ) Service conditions in different zones including service tenii>eratures; 

g) Details of lining used in various zones and sections; 

h) Refractory installation practices used for the boUers/furnaces; 

j) Consumption pattern of refractories, 

k) Applicable standards^ namely> Indian and other standards, design, codes, 
stress considerations, etc; and 

m) Miscellaneous aspects not covered from (a) to (k) above. 

This part of the Handbook covers the typical characteristics of refractories 
used in the different zones of the cement kiln systems of the large cement plants. It 
also covers the temperaturei and other service conditions prevailing in the 
different zones and the recommendations for the use of refractory lining in 
various zones. 

No handbook of this type can be made complete for all times to come at the 
very first attempt. During the course of use of this Handbook, it may be 
possible to make suggestions with regard to improving its utility. All such 
suggestions may be passed on to the Bureau of Indian Standards. These 
suggestions will be taken into consideration while revising the Handbook. The 
*"ggestions with regard to presentation of the Handbook will help in improving 
the presentation of other parts which will be printed subsequently. A complete 
list of Indian Standards for refractories is also given ( see Appendix A ) for the 
convenience of the user.

HANDBOOK FOR REFRACTORIES 

PART 3 REFRACTORIES FOR C»AENT KILN SYSTEM 



1. INTRODUCTION 

!•! Portland cement ii obtained from clinker pro- 
duced by burning a finely ground and blended 
mixture of limestone and clay with or without some 
corrective materials^ such as^ bauxite, laterite or iron 
ore, at temperatures ranging from 1 400 to I 500*C 
in either vertical shaft kilns or rotary kilns. These kilns 
are metallic constructions lined with suitable refrac- 
tories. The refractory lining in these kilns is inten- 
ded to protect the metallic shells as well as the 
operators from the effects of hich temperature, to 
reduce heat losses to the outside environment, and 
to provide the necessary thermochemical conditions 
inside the kilns Tor the appropriate firing of the 
charge material. 

1.2 The cost of refractory lining of kiln system, 
inclusive of materials and installation, amounts to 
less than five percent of the total cost of production. 
This cost is low compared to other cost inputs 
Nevertheless^ it has an overriding effect on the 
economic operation of a plant, if the production 
losses that occur due to the premature failure of 



lining are taken into account. The significance of 
refractory lining in cement kilns has to be viewed in 
this perspective. 

2. PROCESS OPTIONS AND KILN SYSTEMS 

2.1 The manufacturing process options in clinker- 
making are related primarily to the raw material 
characteristics and economic viability of the total 
system alternatives. This leads to a possibility of 
adoption of a wide variety of kiln system. The 
process and system options are broadly classified in 
Fig. 1. Depending on the process route adopted, 
the kiln systems are broadly classified as follows: 

a) wet process kilns ( wet slurry feeding ), 

b) semi-wet process kilns ( nodulised feed from 
wet slurry preparation ), 

c) semi-dry process kilns ( nodulised feed from 

dry mix preparation ), and 

d) dry process kilns ( dry mix powder feeding ).

c) suspension preheater kilns ( with or without

Fio. 4 ZoNATioN IN Typical Dry-Process Rotary Kiln Systbii 



3. ZONATION OF KILN SYSTEMS 

3,1 The concept of kiln zonation has arisen out of 
the fact that the process of cement manufacture 
follows the following stages of thermal treatment: 

a) drying, 

b) preheating, 

c) calcining, 

d) sintering, and 

e) cooling. 

3.1.1 The sintering zone, as depicted in Fig. 2, 
is often extended to cover a transition zone inclusive 
of a security zone, the later often being considered 
as a part of the transition zone itself. 

3«1,2 The division into zones and choice of ref* 
ractories are based, as far as drying, preheating and 
calcining are concerned, on the type of kiln or kiln 
system, since for these stages of the process, there 
are considerable structural diflferences in the various 
parts of the installation. 



3.1.3 The typical service conditions in different 
zones and parts of the rotary kiln systems are given 
in Table I and specifically illustrated in Fig. 3 
and 4 with respect to a typical wet process and 
suspension preheater kiln of dry type which is the 
coinmon form of kiln in use in the industry. 

4. SELECTION OF REFRACTORIES FOR 
TYPICAL AND IMPORTANT ZONES AND 
LOCATIONS 

4.t Drying Zone — This zone is exclusively pre- 
sent in long wet process kilns and is usually equip- 
ped with cross and/or chains for effective heat 
transfer. The lining is subjected to wear and 
abrasion. While standard fireclay bricks or clinker 
bricks have been in me, special fire day bricks with 
high cold crushing strength ( CCS ) ( say, 600 — 
700 kgf/cm^ ) have proved satisfactory. In chain 
sections, special bricks of complicated shape might 
be required to brick round the ends of the chain 
anchoring. For this reason increasing preference is 
given to concrete lining having wear resistance and 
creep resi^ance properties at operational tempera* 
ture range.

4.2 Preheating Zone — For this zone the choice 
of refractories mainly depends on the process. 

4.2*1 Long Wit Prociss Kilns — Abrasion and pre* 
sence of moisture requires the use of a dense, low- 
porosity aluminous firebricks for long wet process 
kilns. Use of insulating bricks, particularly chemi- 
cally bonded, presents a risk due to moisture 
penetration. 

4.2.2 Long Dry Process Kilns — The use of hot face 
insulating bricks is preferred in the long dry process 
kilns. 

4.2.3 Lepol Grate Preheattrs — In the lepol grate 
preheaters, for the drying and heating chambers, 
low porosity aluminous firebricks are used above 
the grate level. A backing of low 'conductivity 
insulating bricks may help in reducing heat losses. 
To form a stable platform high strength castables, 
anchored to the shell, are required. Below the 
grate level, high strength insulating bricks may be 
preferred. Low duty firebricks are recommended 
for the lining of suction chambers. 

4.2.4 Suspension Preheaters — The top three cyc- 
lones and riser pipes of suspension preheaters are 
usually lined with dense low porosity aluminous 
firebricks or equivalent monolithics. A back-up 
insulation lining is often prefetred for reduction of 
heat losses. Ghutei are also lined with dense low 
porosity firebricks. Where it is difficult to instal 
brick HTork; a dense, nfedium duty refractory cast- 
able is used. 



4.3 Calcining Zone 

4.3.1 In the calcining zone of long or suspension 
preheater kilns as well as in the lower cyclones of 
precalciner kilns; dense, low porosity, low iron 
bricks or castables with good alkali resistance are 
preferred. The break-up insulation lining can also 
be considered. 

4.3.2 Precalciner vessels are also lined with high* 
strength, dense, high-alumina spalling resistant 
bricks. The back-up insulation is possible. A 
high-strength castable is required for the burner* 
quarl. 

4.4 Burning and Transition Zone 

4.4.1 Refractories for the burning and transition 
zones must be able to withstand hi^h thermal loads, 
temperature fluctuations, chemical attack and 
abrasion. The transition part of the burning zone 
is subject to large variations in temperature as the 
protective coating is taxed to its limit in this area. 

4.4.2 Depending on the kiln size and severity of 
operations, the^ining material for this zone is 
selected from the following types: 

> , 

a) High alumina bricks of 70 to 75 percent 
alumina content 

b) Silicate bonded magnesite-chrome bricks 

c) Direct bonded magnesite^chrome bricks 

d) Sintered and tar-impregnated dolomite 
bricks 

e) Ma^nesite alumina spinel bricks. 



14 



8P t S7 ( Part 3 ) • 1M7 



4.5 DItclimrge ( Cooling ) Zone 

4.5.1 With variation in protecti\^ clinker cooling, 
tht lining in this zone is subjected to hot clinker, 
flame and dust-laden secondary air^ thermal shock 
and high-temperature abrasion. High-alumink 
bricks with good elasticity and strength characteris- 
tics form the standard lining of discharge zone. 

4*5*2 For end-discharge kilns, silicon carbide 
bricks have proved satisfactory for the nose ring 
owin^ to the;r particularly high resistance to wear. 
Alternatively, monolithic castables with comparable 
properties, securely anchored to the shell by heat- 
resistant steel anchors, may be used with advantage, 

4.6 Coolert 

4.C.1 The refractory linings of cooling units, no 
matter how difficult their design may be, have 
similar requirements for resistance to thermal shock, 
impact, abrasion and erosion. The only lining 
materials that can be considered, therefore, are fire- 
clay bricks and high alumina bricks of high strength 
or suitable castables. 

4«7 Firing Hood and Burner Pipe 

4.7.1 Although brick-lining is not uncommon for 
firing hoods, abrasion resistance and elimination of 
complicated brick cutting can be satisfied by using 
monolithics. The lining of burner pipes is restricted 
to high strength refractory castables for abrasion 
resistance to dust-laden gases.

6. INDIAN STANDARD SPECIFICATIONS 
FOR CEMENT KILN REFRACTORIES 

6*1 The Indian Standard for refractories for cement 
rotary kilitt { IS : 10607-1083 Specification for refrac- 

Sries for cement rotary kilns ) aims at rationalizing 
e requirements of refractory bricks and castables. 
This standard dill not include the basic bricks for 
use in cement kilns due to non-availability of usage 
ilata at the time of formulation of the standard. 
The relevant extracts of this standard are given in 
Table 2. This Indian Standard has recommended 
the use of 3 grades of high alumina and ahimino- 
silicate bricks. Three grades of dense castables 
and one grade of insulating castable for lining the 



entire cement kiln systems. The standard hat alio 
adopted the ISO specification for wedge shaped 
bricks for use in cement kilns ( ISO 5417-1986 
Refractory bricks for use in rotary kilnt — 
Dimensions, which w^s at the draft stage at the time 
of formulation of IS : 10607-1983 }. The relevant 
part of IS : 10607-1983 is given in Table 3.

8« REFRACTORY INSTALLATION 
PRACTICES 

8.1 The adoption of refractory practices primarily 
depends on the following three factors: 

a) Operational safety, 

b) Proper installation, and 

c) Minimization of placement time. 

8*2 Depending on whether a rotary kiln needs to 
be rotated or can be kept stationary at the time of 
lining, the installation practices are further classic 
fied as: 

a) Rotary methods, and 

b) Formwork methods. 

8.2.1 Rotary Methods — In the rotating methods 
the work is carried out at the kiln bottom and the 
lining proceeds on intermittent rotation of the kiln. 
The fixation of the bricks on rotation is done by 
any one of the following techniques: 

a) Screw-jack method, 

b) Glueing, and 

c) Bolting. 

8.2.2 Formwork Method — The curved fortnwork 
methods are safer in operation and permit very 
accurate installation of bricks. In these methods 
the lower half of shell is lined without any parti- 
cular aids and then the upper half is lined with the 
aid of curved formwork. There is a wide choice 
of equipment from simple wooden forms to 
hydraulically operated mechanized forms.
